title: Infectious Diseases
tagline: Fever and sepsis, HIV, tuberculosis, tropical and sexually transmitted infections, infection in healthcare and in weakened immunity, and antimicrobial stewardship
summary: Infections remain a leading cause of illness and death worldwide. This course approaches infection clinically and from the population side: the febrile patient and sepsis, HIV and tuberculosis, malaria and other tropical infections, sexually transmitted infections, infections acquired in healthcare and in people with weakened immunity, and antimicrobial resistance, stewardship and outbreak investigation.
overview: Every infection is caused by a living organism with its own biology and epidemiology, acting on a host with particular defences and exposures. This course teaches the clinical reasoning that follows from that: from a fever to its source, from the exposure history to the likely organism, from the immune defect to the infections it permits, and from empirical to targeted treatment.

It opens with fever and sepsis: how to recognise and treat sepsis early, find and control its source, and investigate fever without an obvious cause. Two chapters cover the great chronic infections: HIV, from virology and diagnosis to antiretroviral therapy, prevention and opportunistic infections; and tuberculosis, from pathogenesis to latent infection, standard treatment and drug resistance. The returning traveller and the tropics follow, with malaria first, then dengue, enteric fever, emerging viral infections and helminths, and then sexually transmitted infections, from the sexual history to syphilis serology and partner notification.

The last three chapters turn to infections that medicine itself shapes. Healthcare-associated infections covers device and surgical-site infection, Clostridioides difficile and resistant organisms. Infection in weakened immunity matches each immune defect to its organisms, with neutropenic sepsis, transplant infections and the risks of biological drugs and asplenia. The course closes with antimicrobial resistance, pharmacokinetic principles, stewardship and outbreak investigation. Guidance is UK-first (NICE, UKHSA, BHIVA, BASHH) with WHO for the global picture; doses are given as principles, because recommendations change and local guidance must be followed.
outcomes: Recognise sepsis and septic shock using current definitions and early warning scores, deliver initial management promptly, identify and control the source, and approach fever without an obvious cause systematically.

Describe HIV virology and natural history, choose and interpret HIV tests, explain the principles of antiretroviral therapy and prevention (U=U, PrEP, PEP), and recognise and prevent the main opportunistic infections.
Explain the pathogenesis of tuberculosis, diagnose pulmonary, extrapulmonary and latent infection, outline standard and drug-resistant treatment with monitoring, and apply contact tracing.
Assess the returning traveller with fever, diagnose and grade malaria and start emergency treatment, and recognise dengue, enteric fever, viral haemorrhagic fevers and important helminth infections.
Take a sexual history, diagnose and manage chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, herpes and other common sexually transmitted infections, interpret syphilis serology, and arrange partner notification.
Explain how healthcare-associated infections arise and are prevented, manage device-related and surgical-site infections, and diagnose and treat Clostridioides difficile infection.

Match immune defects to likely organisms, manage neutropenic sepsis, describe the timeline of infection after transplantation, and apply screening, vaccination and prophylaxis before immunosuppressive treatment and after splenectomy.

Explain the mechanisms and spread of antimicrobial resistance, use pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic principles and susceptibility data to choose antibiotics, apply stewardship interventions, and investigate an outbreak step by step.

history.title: The tubercle bacillus
history.detail: On 24 March 1882 Robert Koch announced in Berlin that tuberculosis is caused by a bacillus, which he had stained, grown in culture and used to reproduce the disease in animals. Effective drug treatment came only in the 1940s.

history.title: The mosquito theory of malaria
history.detail: Alphonse Laveran had seen malaria parasites in human blood in 1880. In 1897–1898 Ronald Ross showed that mosquitoes transmit malaria parasites (in birds), and Giovanni Battista Grassi and colleagues showed that Anopheles mosquitoes transmit human malaria, opening the way to control by attacking the vector.

history.title: The magic bullet
history.detail: Paul Ehrlich and Sahachiro Hata introduced arsphenamine (Salvarsan) for syphilis, the first synthetic drug designed to target a microbe inside the body. Ehrlich called the idea a 'magic bullet', and his systematic screening of compounds founded chemotherapy.

history.title: Penicillin noticed
history.detail: Alexander Fleming published his observation that a Penicillium mould killed staphylococci on a culture plate. A decade later Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley in Oxford purified penicillin and showed in 1940–1941 that it cured infections in mice and people, beginning the antibiotic era.

history.title: Streptomycin — and its price
history.detail: Albert Schatz, working in Selman Waksman's laboratory, isolated streptomycin from a soil bacterium, the first drug active against tuberculosis. The Medical Research Council trial of 1948 showed its benefit and also the rapid emergence of resistance, which led to combination therapy for tuberculosis.

history.title: Field trial of the polio vaccine
history.detail: On 12 April 1955 the results of the 1954 field trial of Jonas Salk's inactivated polio vaccine, led by Thomas Francis and involving about 1.8 million children, were announced: the vaccine was safe and effective. Albert Sabin's oral vaccine followed in the early 1960s, and together they made polio eradication possible.

history.title: A new syndrome reported
history.detail: On 5 June 1981 the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report described Pneumocystis pneumonia in five previously healthy young men in Los Angeles, reported by Michael Gottlieb and colleagues. The causative retrovirus was identified in 1983–1984 by the groups of Luc Montagnier and Robert Gallo, and named HIV in 1986.

history.title: Combination antiretroviral therapy
history.detail: At the International AIDS Conference in Vancouver in 1996, trials of combinations of antiretroviral drugs including protease inhibitors were presented, and David Ho and others argued for early, potent combination therapy. Deaths from AIDS fell sharply where treatment became available, and HIV became a manageable chronic infection.

history.title: Ebola and the limits of response
history.detail: The West African Ebola epidemic of 2014–2016 caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, exposing weaknesses in health systems and in international response. A ring vaccination trial in Guinea in 2015 showed that the rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine protected against Ebola.
